paper_metadata.title: A Comparative Analysis of Hybrid Quantum Neural Networks in Binary Credit Defaulting Tasks

summary: The paper studies a hybrid quantum-classical neural network for binary credit default prediction on a dataset of over 17,000 cases with 20 features, reduced to 10 via LDA. The quantum model, built from a continuous-variable variational circuit in PennyLane/Strawberry Fields, achieved 97.63% training accuracy and 96.21% validation accuracy after 40 epochs, compared with 91.22% training and 91.11% validation accuracy for the classical neural network, but it required about 70 seconds per step versus 7 seconds for the classical model.

experiments.description: Hybrid quantum-classical neural network for binary credit default prediction using a continuous-variable variational quantum circuit with classical preprocessing and a classical neural baseline.

algorithm.variant: Hybrid quantum neural network / QCNN with continuous-variable variational circuit
algorithm.ansatz: Interferometer–squeezer–interferometer followed by displacement and Kerr gates; repeated for five blocks
algorithm.convergence_criteria: trained for at least 30 epochs; additional 10 epochs for quantum model

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Classical layer output encoded using amplitude embedding from PennyLane; original 20 features reduced to 10 via LDA before quantum layer
problem_formulation.objective_function: Binary classification of credit defaulting (predict default vs non-default)

problem_instance.description: Binary credit default prediction on credit card holder data
problem_instance.dataset_name: Synthetic oversampling for credit card default prediction (Fransiscus Pratikto, 2023)

dataset_specification.description: 20 predictor features and one binary target; 16,143 normal cases and 1,564 default cases before undersampling; 10% test split

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Converted Excel to CSV; inspected data types and statistics; dropped null-value columns and client ID; undersampled normal cases to 3:1 ratio vs default cases; standardized features with StandardScaler; LDA reduced 20 features to 10; one-hot encoded output variables
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Training/validation accuracy and loss tracked over epochs; 10% of data used for testing; classical and quantum models compared after 30 epochs, with quantum model also run for 40 epochs

implementation_details.classical_solver: TensorFlow/Keras Sequential/Dense classical neural network baseline; Adam optimizer
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Pandas/NumPy data handling; StandardScaler normalization; LDA feature reduction; undersampling for class imbalance
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Accuracy and loss comparison between classical and quantum models

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: quantum model loss decreased with high variability early, then leveled out after about 15 epochs

speedup_claims.conditions: same binary credit default prediction task; classical model trained for 30 epochs and quantum model for 30-40 epochs
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports higher accuracy for the quantum model but longer runtime per step (~70s vs ~7s). No asymptotic or wall-clock speedup is demonstrated.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Not enough hardware/complexity data; the paper reports a continuous-variable variational circuit implemented in PennyLane/Strawberry Fields with no qubit count or device specification.
limiting_factors: No qubit count or circuit depth reported
Quantum model is slower per step (70 s) than classical baseline (7 s)
Comparison is accuracy-focused rather than demonstrating practical quantum advantage

notes: No explicit qubit count, circuit depth, shot count, or hardware device is reported in the paper; the quantum layer is described as a continuous-variable variational circuit built with PennyLane/Strawberry Fields.
speedup_order set to none_proven because the paper reports higher accuracy but longer runtime, not an asymptotic speedup analysis.

The paper reports higher validation accuracy for the quantum model (96.21% / 97.63% training) than the classical neural network (91.11% validation, 91.22% training), but also substantially longer runtime per step (70 s vs 7 s).
This does not establish practical quantum advantage under Hoefler-style criteria.
